claim: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are small cationic molecules best known as mediators of the innate defence against microbial infection.
source: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are small cationic molecules best known as mediators of the innate defence against microbial infection.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the general properties and function of AMPs.

claim: In vitro and ex vivo evidence suggest AMPs' capacity to kill cancer cells.
source: While in vitro and ex vivo evidence suggest AMPs' capacity to kill cancer cells, in vivo demonstration of an anti-tumour role of endogenous AMPs is lacking.
evidence: This claim references existing literature on AMP anticancer activity in vitro and ex vivo.

claim: In vivo demonstration of an anti-tumour role of endogenous AMPs is lacking.
source: While in vitro and ex vivo evidence suggest AMPs' capacity to kill cancer cells, in vivo demonstration of an anti-tumour role of endogenous AMPs is lacking.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the existing literature that the study aims to address.

claim: Defensin plays a role in the control of tumour progression in a Drosophila model of tumourigenesis.
source: Using a Drosophila model of tumourigenesis, we demonstrate a role for the AMP Defensin in the control of tumour progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches including genetic mutants and knockdowns.

claim: Tumour Necrosis Factor mediates exposure of phosphatidylserine (PS) in tumour cells.
source: Our results reveal that Tumour Necrosis Factor mediates exposure of phosphatidylserine (PS), which makes tumour cells selectively sensitive to the action of Defensin remotely secreted from tracheal and fat tissues.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing PS exposure is dependent on TNF/Eiger.

claim: PS exposure makes tumour cells selectively sensitive to the action of Defensin.
source: Our results reveal that Tumour Necrosis Factor mediates exposure of phosphatidylserine (PS), which makes tumour cells selectively sensitive to the action of Defensin remotely secreted from tracheal and fat tissues.
evidence: This is supported by data showing Defensin binds to PS-enriched areas and that TNF is required for Defensin-induced cell death.

claim: Defensin is remotely secreted from tracheal and fat tissues.
source: Our results reveal that Tumour Necrosis Factor mediates exposure of phosphatidylserine (PS), which makes tumour cells selectively sensitive to the action of Defensin remotely secreted from tracheal and fat tissues.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data and immunostaining showing Defensin expression in fat body and trachea.

claim: Defensin binds tumour cells in PS-enriched areas.
source: Defensin binds tumour cells in PS-enriched areas, provoking cell death and tumour regression.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data showing Defensin enrichment in Annexin V positive areas.

claim: Defensin binding to tumour cells provokes cell death and tumour regression.
source: Defensin binds tumour cells in PS-enriched areas, provoking cell death and tumour regression.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased tumour size and decreased cell death in defensin mutants, and rescue experiments.

claim: Tumourigenesis triggers inflammation and activation of the immune system in mammals and flies, leading to tumour cell death.
source: In mammals and flies, tumourigenesis triggers inflammation and activation of the immune system, leading to tumour cell death (Cordero et al., 2010; Parameswaran and Patial, 2010; Parisi et al., 2014; Teng et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tumour Necrosis Factor (TNF) is an important player in tumour/immune interactions and has pleiotropic effects on tumours, including induction of cell death.
source: Tumour Necrosis Factor (TNF) is an important player in these tumour/immune interactions and has pleiotropic effects on tumours, including induction of cell death (Ham et al., 2016; Parameswaran and Patial, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The function of TNF in inducing tumour cell death is conserved in Drosophila.
source: This function is conserved in Drosophila, where the single TNF homolog Eiger (Egr), produced by tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs), has been shown to drive cell death of neoplastic tumours, generated in larval imaginal discs by the loss of apico-basal complex components such as Disc large 1, Scribble or Lethal giant larvae (Cordero et al., 2010; Parisi et al., 2014; Parvy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: Eiger (Egr) is the single TNF homolog in Drosophila.
source: This function is conserved in Drosophila, where the single TNF homolog Eiger (Egr), produced by tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs), has been shown to drive cell death of neoplastic tumours, generated in larval imaginal discs by the loss of apico-basal complex components such as Disc large 1, Scribble or Lethal giant larvae (Cordero et al., 2010; Parisi et al., 2014; Parvy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila genetics.

claim: Eiger is produced by tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs).
source: This function is conserved in Drosophila, where the single TNF homolog Eiger (Egr), produced by tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs), has been shown to drive cell death of neoplastic tumours, generated in larval imaginal discs by the loss of apico-basal complex components such as Disc large 1, Scribble or Lethal giant larvae (Cordero et al., 2010; Parisi et al., 2014; Parvy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Eiger drives cell death of neoplastic tumours generated by loss of apico-basal complex components.
source: This function is conserved in Drosophila, where the single TNF homolog Eiger (Egr), produced by tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs), has been shown to drive cell death of neoplastic tumours, generated in larval imaginal discs by the loss of apico-basal complex components such as Disc large 1, Scribble or Lethal giant larvae (Cordero et al., 2010; Parisi et al., 2014; Parvy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tumours from disc large 1 Drosophila mutant larvae activate Toll pathway in the Drosophila fat body in an Egr-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, we have previously reported that tumours from disc large 1 Drosophila mutant larvae (dlg40.2 hereafter referred to as dlg), activate Toll pathway in the Drosophila fat body in an Egr-dependent manner, and this immune activation is necessary for TNF-dependent tumour cell death (Parisi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Toll pathway activation in the fat body is necessary for TNF-dependent tumour cell death.
source: Moreover, we have previously reported that tumours from disc large 1 Drosophila mutant larvae (dlg40.2 hereafter referred to as dlg), activate Toll pathway in the Drosophila fat body in an Egr-dependent manner, and this immune activation is necessary for TNF-dependent tumour cell death (Parisi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The mechanisms by which activation of an immune response in the fat body executes tumour cell death remain unknown.
source: However, the mechanisms by which activation of an immune response in the fat body executes tumour cell death remain unknown (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Toll pathway is well known to play a central role in the innate immune response to infection in Drosophila and mammals.
source: In Drosophila as in mammals, Toll pathway is well known to play a central role in the innate immune response to infection (Lemaitre et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Downstream effectors of the Toll pathway include antimicrobial peptides (AMPs).
source: Downstream effectors of the Toll pathway include antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), which possess microbicidal activities against various pathogens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Toll pathway.

claim: AMPs possess microbicidal activities against various pathogens.
source: Downstream effectors of the Toll pathway include antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), which possess microbicidal activities against various pathogens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMP function.

claim: AMPs display potent antimicrobial activity in vitro by disrupting negatively-charged microbial membranes.
source: They display potent antimicrobial activity in vitro by disrupting negatively-charged microbial membranes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMP mechanism of action.

claim: Many AMPs kill pathogens by inserting into the lipid bilayer and disrupting the membrane integrity.
source: While intracellular activities have been reported, many AMPs kill pathogens by inserting into the lipid bilayer and disrupting the membrane integrity (Brogden, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Host cells are protected from AMP because they are positively charged and contain cholesterol.
source: Host cells are instead protected from AMP as they are positively charged and contain cholesterol (Brender et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In vitro studies have revealed AMPs capacity to kill cancer cells.
source: In vitro studies have revealed AMPs capacity to kill cancer cells (Deslouches and Di, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Whether cancer-killing activity is a natural function of AMPs is unknown.
source: However, whether this cancer-killing activity is a natural function of AMPs is unknown, as there are no reports on an in vivo paradigm addressing such question.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The Toll pathway is activated in dlg mutant tumour bearing larvae.
source: Since the Toll pathway is activated in dlg mutant tumour bearing larvae and is required for optimal TNF-induced tumour cell death (Parisi et al., 2014), we hypothesised that AMPs may be involved in this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Toll pathway is required for optimal TNF-induced tumour cell death in dlg mutant larvae.
source: Since the Toll pathway is activated in dlg mutant tumour bearing larvae and is required for optimal TNF-induced tumour cell death (Parisi et al., 2014), we hypothesised that AMPs may be involved in this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Drosophila defensin is induced in the fat body and tracheal system of dlg mutant tumour bearing larvae.
source: Here we show that Drosophila defensin is induced in the fat body and tracheal system of dlg mutant tumour bearing larvae.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR and immunostaining data.

claim: Defensin is consistently associated to dying tumour cells.
source: We find Defensin consistently associated to dying tumour cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing colocalization of Defensin with apoptotic markers.

claim: Systemic and tissue specific knockdown of Defensin demonstrates a non-redundant role of the AMP in controlling tumour growth through the induction of tumour cell death.
source: Critically, systemic and tissue specific knockdown of Defensin demonstrates a non-redundant role of the AMP in controlling tumour growth through the induction of tumour cell death.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased tumour size and decreased cell death upon Defensin knockdown.

claim: Anti-tumoural Defensin production relies on TNF-dependent activation of both Toll and Imd pathway.
source: Anti-tumoural Defensin production relies on TNF-dependent activation of both Toll and Imd pathway.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced Defensin expression in Egr, Toll, and Imd pathway mutants.

claim: dlg mutant tumours expose PS in response to haemocyte-derived TNF.
source: Our results demonstrate that dlg mutant tumours expose PS in response to haemocyte-derived TNF and that Defensin is present in PS enriched area on the tumour surface.
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data showing PS exposure is dependent on Egr from haemocytes.

claim: Defensin is present in PS enriched area on the tumour surface.
source: Our results demonstrate that dlg mutant tumours expose PS in response to haemocyte-derived TNF and that Defensin is present in PS enriched area on the tumour surface.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data showing Defensin enrichment in Annexin V positive areas.

claim: Lack of TNF prevents PS exposure in tumours.
source: Finally, we find that lack of TNF prevents PS exposure in tumours and makes them insensitive to the action of Defensin.
evidence: This is supported by data showing loss of PS exposure in dlg;egr double mutants.

claim: Lack of TNF makes tumours insensitive to the action of Defensin.
source: Finally, we find that lack of TNF prevents PS exposure in tumours and makes them insensitive to the action of Defensin.
evidence: This is supported by data showing Defensin injection cannot induce cell death in egr mutant tumours.

claim: Fat bodies of dlg mutant larvae show consistent and statistically significant upregulation of defensin compared to wild-type.
source: Results showed consistent and statistically significant upregulation of defensin in fat bodies of dlg larvae compared to wild-type ones (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Other Toll-dependent AMPs (drosomycin and attacin A) display a trend to be increased in dlg mutant fat bodies, though data were highly variable amongst biological replicates.
source: Other Toll-dependent AMPs display a trend to be increased (drosomycin and attacin A), even though data were highly variable amongst biological replicates, while other AMPs were not transcriptionally regulated (drosocyn, cecropin A1) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Some AMPs (drosocyn, cecropin A1) were not transcriptionally regulated in dlg mutant fat bodies.
source: Other Toll-dependent AMPs display a trend to be increased (drosomycin and attacin A), even though data were highly variable amongst biological replicates, while other AMPs were not transcriptionally regulated (drosocyn, cecropin A1) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Human β-Defensin-1 displays anticancer activity in vitro.
source: Interestingly, human β-Defensin-1 displays anticancer activity in vitro (Bullard et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2006), and deletion of human def appears prevalent in some cancer types (Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of human def appears prevalent in some cancer types.
source: Interestingly, human β-Defensin-1 displays anticancer activity in vitro (Bullard et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2006), and deletion of human def appears prevalent in some cancer types (Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Defensin upregulation in dlg larvae is independent of the presence of microbes.
source: Using dlg larvae reared on antibiotics, we confirmed that defensin upregulation was independent of the presence of microbes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from larvae reared on antibiotics shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Larvae bearing dlg imaginal discs tumours induced by RNAi display increased defensin expression.
source: Moreover, larvae bearing dlg imaginal discs tumours induced by RNAi (en >UAS-dcr2; UAS-dlg-IR) also displayed increased defensin expression, confirming def gene induction as a consequence of dlg-driven epithelial transformation rather than whole body dl loss (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: def gene induction is a consequence of dlg-driven epithelial transformation rather than whole body dlg loss.
source: Moreover, larvae bearing dlg imaginal discs tumours induced by RNAi (en >UAS-dcr2; UAS-dlg-IR) also displayed increased defensin expression, confirming def gene induction as a consequence of dlg-driven epithelial transformation rather than whole body dl loss (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi experiment showing tissue-specific dlg knockdown induces defensin.

claim: Defensin contributes to resistance to systemic infection to certain Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Survival analysis of defsk3 flies confirmed that this AMP contribute to resist systemic infection to certain Gram-positive bacteria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Levashina et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: dlg;def double mutants display a significant increase in tumour size compared to dlg mutant animals.
source: Compared to dlg mutant animals, dlg;def double mutants displayed a significant increase in tumour size (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by tumour volume quantification data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tumour growth is limited by apoptotic tumour cell death as revealed by Dcp1 staining.
source: Tumour growth is limited by apoptotic tumour cell death as revealed by Dcp1 staining (Parisi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and is consistent with the current study's data.

claim: Tumours from dlg;def double mutants display a very strong decrease in apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, tumours from dlg;def double mutants display a very strong decrease in apoptosis (Figure 2B–E'), suggesting that increased tumour size in absence of Defensin is due to a decrease in tumour cell death.
evidence: This is supported by Dcp1 staining quantification shown in Figure 2B-E'.

claim: Increased tumour size in absence of Defensin is due to a decrease in tumour cell death.
source: Interestingly, tumours from dlg;def double mutants display a very strong decrease in apoptosis (Figure 2B–E'), suggesting that increased tumour size in absence of Defensin is due to a decrease in tumour cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tumour size increases while apoptosis decreases in def mutants.

claim: dlg and dlg,def mutant tumours have similar proliferation rates.
source: This was further supported by the similar proliferation rates measured in dlg and dlg,def mutant tumours as per quantification of anti-phophoHistone H3 staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E').
evidence: This is supported by pH3 staining quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-E'.

claim: The effect of Def on tumour size and cell death are observed when dlg and dlg,def larvae are reared in sterile conditions.
source: Importantly, the effect of Def on tumour size and cell death were still observed when dlg and dlg,def larvae were reared in sterile conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–J') and further confirmed upon ubiquitous knock down of def using RNA interference (IR) (Figure 2F–J').
evidence: This is supported by data from larvae reared on antibiotics shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-J'.

claim: Ubiquitous knockdown of def confirms the effect on tumour size and cell death.
source: Importantly, the effect of Def on tumour size and cell death were still observed when dlg and dlg,def larvae were reared in sterile conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–J') and further confirmed upon ubiquitous knock down of def using RNA interference (IR) (Figure 2F–J').
evidence: This is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 2F-J'.

claim: Fat body overexpression of def significantly rescues tumour volume and tumour cell death of dlg;defsk3 double mutant animals.
source: Furthermore, fat body overexpression of def significantly rescued tumour volume and tumour cell death of dlg;defsk3 double mutant animals (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2K and L.

claim: Larval injection of a synthetic Defensin peptide increases tumour cell death of dlg or dlg;defsk3 imaginal discs.
source: Additionally, larval injection of a synthetic Defensin peptide increased tumour cell death of dlg or dlg;defsk3 imaginal discs (Figure 2M), while it had no effect on tissues from wild-type larvae, indicating that Defensin can selectively promote cell death of tumour cells.
evidence: This is supported by injection experiment data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Defensin injection has no effect on tissues from wild-type larvae.
source: Additionally, larval injection of a synthetic Defensin peptide increased tumour cell death of dlg or dlg;defsk3 imaginal discs (Figure 2M), while it had no effect on tissues from wild-type larvae, indicating that Defensin can selectively promote cell death of tumour cells.
evidence: This is supported by injection experiment data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Defensin can selectively promote cell death of tumour cells.
source: Additionally, larval injection of a synthetic Defensin peptide increased tumour cell death of dlg or dlg;defsk3 imaginal discs (Figure 2M), while it had no effect on tissues from wild-type larvae, indicating that Defensin can selectively promote cell death of tumour cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Defensin affects tumour cells but not wild-type cells.

claim: Defensin is not produced by imaginal discs or tumours.
source: Previous studies have shown that Defensin is not produced by imaginal discs or tumours (Bunker et al., 2015; Külshammer et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the context of infection, Defensin can be produced by the fat body as well the tracheal and gut epithelium.
source: In the context of infection, Defensin can be produced by the fat body as well the tracheal and gut epithelium (Tzou et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The fat body and the trachea are the main sources of defensin in tumour bearing animals.
source: We observed that the fat body, homologue to the mammalian liver and adipose tissue, and the trachea, a network of tubes transporting oxygen to cells that resembles the mammalian vasculature, were the main sources of defensin in these animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from dissected tissues shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The fat body is homologue to the mammalian liver and adipose tissue.
source: We observed that the fat body, homologue to the mammalian liver and adipose tissue, and the trachea, a network of tubes transporting oxygen to cells that resembles the mammalian vasculature, were the main sources of defensin in these animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila anatomy.

claim: The trachea is a network of tubes transporting oxygen to cells that resembles the mammalian vasculature.
source: We observed that the fat body, homologue to the mammalian liver and adipose tissue, and the trachea, a network of tubes transporting oxygen to cells that resembles the mammalian vasculature, were the main sources of defensin in these animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila anatomy.

claim: Defensin immunostaining supports that fat body and trachea are the main sources of defensin in tumour bearing animals.
source: This was also supported by Defensin immunostaining, (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Targeted IR knockdown of defensin in fat body and trachea confirms the domains of endogenous gene expression.
source: Transcript assessment upon targeted IR knock down of defensin in the respective tissues further confirmed the domains of endogenous gene expression (Figure 3D and I).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from tissue-specific knockdowns shown in Figure 3D and I.

claim: Knocking down defensin expression specifically in the fat body of dlg animals results in increased tumour size and decreased tumour cell death.
source: Importantly, knocking down defensin expression specifically in the fat body or the trachea of dlg animals, resulted in increased tumour size and decreased tumour cell death (Figure 3E–H' and J–M') confirming the non-redundant functional requirement of defensin in both tissues to efficiently promote tumour cell death.
evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific knockdown data shown in Figure 3E-H'.

claim: Knocking down defensin expression specifically in the trachea of dlg animals results in increased tumour size and decreased tumour cell death.
source: Importantly, knocking down defensin expression specifically in the fat body or the trachea of dlg animals, resulted in increased tumour size and decreased tumour cell death (Figure 3E–H' and J–M') confirming the non-redundant functional requirement of defensin in both tissues to efficiently promote tumour cell death.
evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific knockdown data shown in Figure 3J-M'.

claim: Defensin has a non-redundant functional requirement in both fat body and trachea to efficiently promote tumour cell death.
source: Importantly, knocking down defensin expression specifically in the fat body or the trachea of dlg animals, resulted in increased tumour size and decreased tumour cell death (Figure 3E–H' and J–M') confirming the non-redundant functional requirement of defensin in both tissues to efficiently promote tumour cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockdown in either tissue affects tumour phenotype.

claim: AMPs targeting of pathogens involves the recognition of negatively charged molecules exposed on the cell surface.
source: AMPs targeting of pathogens, involves the recognition of negatively charged molecules exposed on the cell surface (Yeaman and Yount, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Selective action of cationic AMP is attributed to their ability to interact with negatively charged membrane such as those found in bacteria.
source: Selective action of cationic AMP is attributed to their ability to interact with negatively charged membrane such as those found in bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMP mechanism of action.

claim: Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a negatively charged phospholipid, normally restricted to the inner leaflet of the cell membrane.
source: Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a negatively charged phospholipid, normally restricted to the inner leaflet of the cell membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell membrane biology.

claim: PS can be exposed on the outer leaflet in apoptotic cells, which tags these cells for phagocytosis.
source: However, PS can be exposed on the outer leaflet for example in apoptotic cells, which tags these cells for phagocytosis (Birge et al., 2016; Shklyar et al., 2013; Tung et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PS exposure has been shown to occur independently of apoptosis in many cancer cell types.
source: Moreover, PS exposure has been shown to occur independently of apoptosis in many cancer cell types (Riedl et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: dlg tumours display high levels of Annexin V staining.
source: Our data revealed that dlg but not wild-type tissues, displayed high levels of Annexin V staining (Figure 7A and F; compare to E), indicating increased exposure of PS by dlg tumours.
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 7A and F.

claim: Wild-type tissues do not display high levels of Annexin V staining.
source: Our data revealed that dlg but not wild-type tissues, displayed high levels of Annexin V staining (Figure 7A and F; compare to E), indicating increased exposure of PS by dlg tumours.
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: dlg tumours show increased exposure of PS.
source: Our data revealed that dlg but not wild-type tissues, displayed high levels of Annexin V staining (Figure 7A and F; compare to E), indicating increased exposure of PS by dlg tumours.
evidence: This is inferred from Annexin V staining, which binds to PS.

claim: Defensin is enriched in Annexin V+ve areas on dlg tumours.
source: We next looked at the ability of Defensin to specifically associate with tumour cells exposing PS and found that Defensin was enriched in Annexin V+ve areas on dlg tumours (Figure 7A–A'' and B–B'').
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 7A-A'' and B-B''.

claim: Quantification confirms that Def staining colocalizes with Annexin V staining.
source: This was confirmed by quantification of the amount of Def staining colocalising with Annexin V staining (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Defensin produced by immune responsive tissues binds specifically to tumour cells and this ability correlates with their exposure of PS.
source: Thus, Defensin produced by immune responsive tissues binds specifically to tumour cells and this ability correlated with their exposure of PS.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization of Defensin with PS-exposing areas on tumours.

claim: Circulating macrophage-like cells in Drosophila, called haemocytes, bind to dlg mutant tumours and contribute to cell death.
source: Previous studies have shown that circulating macrophage-like cells in Drosophila, called haemocytes, bind to dlg mutant tumours and contribute to cell death (Parisi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Haemocyte-mediated cell death is mediated by the release of Egr from haemocytes.
source: This process is mediated by the release of Egr from haemocytes (Cordero et al., 2010; Parisi et al., 2014), which then activates the JNK pathway in target cells to promote apoptosis (Igaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Egr activates the JNK pathway in target cells to promote apoptosis.
source: This process is mediated by the release of Egr from haemocytes (Cordero et al., 2010; Parisi et al., 2014), which then activates the JNK pathway in target cells to promote apoptosis (Igaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Toll pathway activation in tumour bearing animals requires Egr.
source: Moreover, Toll pathway activation in tumour bearing animals also requires Egr (Parisi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Defensin upregulation observed in dlg animals is lost in dlg;egr3 double mutants.
source: Accordingly, we found that defensin upregulation observed in dlg animals was lost in dlg;egr3 double mutants (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Egr is required for PS exposure in dlg tumours.
source: We next tested whether PS exposure in tumours was dependent on Eiger, and observed an almost complete loss of cell-surface PS in dlg;egr3 tumours (Figure 7E–G). Therefore, Egr is required for PS exposure in these tumours.
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Specific egr knockdown in haemocytes results in a strong decrease in cell surface-exposed PS in dlg mutant tumours.
source: We then analysed PS exposure in dlg mutant tumours, upon specific egr knockdown in haemocytes (dlg;hml >egr-IR), and observed a strong decrease in cell surface-exposed PS compared to control tumours (dlg;hml >ctrl-IR) (Figure 7H–J).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 7H-J.

claim: PS exposure in tumour cells is likely triggered by the release of Egr from haemocytes.
source: This indicates that PS exposure in tumour cells is likely triggered by the release of Egr from haemocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that haemocyte-specific egr knockdown reduces PS exposure.

claim: Def-HA is expressed in the trachea and fat body of dlg,egr3 mutant animals.
source: Consistently with the observed basal and overexpressed Def-HA expression pattern in wild type tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), Def-HA was expressed in the trachea and fat body of dlg,egr3 mutant animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: No detectable association of Def-HA to the surface of dlg,egr3 tumours was found.
source: However, we did not find any detectable association of Def-HA to the surface of dlg,egr3 tumours (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,C').
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,C'.

claim: Egr-dependent signalling and PS exposure are intact in dlg;def and dlg;imd mutants.
source: Importantly, Egr-dependent signalling and PS exposure were intact in dlg;def and dlg;imd mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) indicating that both events precede the action of Defensin in dlg tumours.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Egr-dependent signalling and PS exposure precede the action of Defensin in dlg tumours.
source: Importantly, Egr-dependent signalling and PS exposure were intact in dlg;def and dlg;imd mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) indicating that both events precede the action of Defensin in dlg tumours.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these events occur even without Defensin.

claim: Defensin injection promotes tumour cell death in dlg mutant tumours.
source: To further assess whether Egr was required for Defensin-induced tumour cell death, we injected synthetic Defensin peptide into control, dlg or dlg;egr3 mutant larvae. While, Defensin injection was able to robustly promote tumour cell death in dlg mutant tumours, it was unable to affect tumours derived from Egr-deficient animals, further demonstrating the requirement of Egr for tumour cell death induced by Defensin (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by injection experiment data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Defensin injection is unable to affect tumours derived from Egr-deficient animals.
source: To further assess whether Egr was required for Defensin-induced tumour cell death, we injected synthetic Defensin peptide into control, dlg or dlg;egr3 mutant larvae. While, Defensin injection was able to robustly promote tumour cell death in dlg mutant tumours, it was unable to affect tumours derived from Egr-deficient animals, further demonstrating the requirement of Egr for tumour cell death induced by Defensin (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by injection experiment data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Egr is required for tumour cell death induced by Defensin.
source: To further assess whether Egr was required for Defensin-induced tumour cell death, we injected synthetic Defensin peptide into control, dlg or dlg;egr3 mutant larvae. While, Defensin injection was able to robustly promote tumour cell death in dlg mutant tumours, it was unable to affect tumours derived from Egr-deficient animals, further demonstrating the requirement of Egr for tumour cell death induced by Defensin (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Defensin cannot induce cell death without Egr.

claim: Tumours induced by the loss of scribble show significant cell surface PS exposure.
